claims: A while loop repeatedly runs its body as long as a loop condition stays true, re-checking the condition before each iteration.
After each pass through the body, the loop expression is evaluated again to decide whether to continue.
If the loop expression is true, the body runs again; if it is false, the loop terminates.
A loop whose condition never becomes false runs forever — an infinite loop — so the body must make progress toward ending the condition.
attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §5.1 While loop

artifact.df: A programming construct that repeats a block of code based on a specified criterion.
artifact.eg: Using a while loop to process user input until a specific command is entered.
artifact.mi: Thinking a loop only runs once per condition check.
artifact.cx: The construct repeatedly runs its body as long as a loop condition stays true, re-checking the condition before each iteration.

artifact.df: A loop that keeps running because its condition never turns false.
artifact.eg: A file-reading loop that never advances the file position can keep printing the same line forever.
artifact.mi: It is any loop that runs a lot of times.
artifact.cx: A loop can run many times and still end normally; it becomes infinite only when the stopping condition never changes.

claims: File I/O lets a program read information from and write information into files; a file is accessed by opening it, working with its contents, and closing it.
open() returns a file object that the program then reads from or writes to.
read() reads the entire contents of a file and returns a single string.
readline() returns the next single line, while readlines() returns a list with every line of the file.
attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §14.1 Reading from files

artifact.q: After a script finishes copying data from a file, what should it do to finish the file-use cycle properly?
artifact.ex: Closing the file object completes the open-work-close cycle described for file input and output. The plausible misconception is to call another read method, but those methods are for getting content, not finishing the access step.

artifact.q: What is the primary action performed by the open() function?
artifact.ex: open() returns a file object that the program then reads from or writes to. The misconception is thinking open() immediately performs the read or write operation; it only establishes the connection.

claims: A dictionary stores key-value pairs and looks up each value by its key rather than by a numeric position.

attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §10.1 Dictionary basics

artifact.df: A mapping structure that stores values under labels instead of positions.
artifact.eg: A class roster can pair each student name with a score or room number.
artifact.mi: It is just an ordered list with fancy punctuation.
artifact.cx: It uses keys to find values, so the data is labeled rather than ordered.

artifact.df: The process of associating a unique identifier with a piece of data.
artifact.eg: Storing student scores where the student ID is the key and the score is the value.
artifact.mi: Thinking that the data must be stored in a strictly sequential, ordered manner.
artifact.cx: Data is stored based on a label (key) rather than a numerical position.

claims: A function is a named, reusable block of code defined with def that runs only when it is called; variables created inside it are local to that call.
A function is defined with the def keyword, a name, parentheses, and a colon, with an indented body.
A variable's scope is the part of the program where it can be accessed.
A variable created inside a function has local scope and cannot be accessed outside the function.
A variable created outside any function has global scope and can be accessed anywhere in the program.
attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §6.1 Defining functions; §6.3 Variable scope

artifact.q: In a small Python program, a student defines a helper with def, creates a variable inside that helper, and then tries to use that same variable after the call ends. Which statement best describes what happens?
op: It has local scope, so it cannot be accessed outside the function.
It becomes global scope after the function finishes running.
It is available anywhere because it was defined with def.
It can be accessed only from other functions in the program.
artifact.ex: Correct: variables created inside a function have local scope and cannot be accessed outside that function. The common misconception is that a name defined during a call becomes available everywhere after the call, but scope does not work that way.

artifact.q: Which statement accurately describes the scope of a variable defined within a function?
op: It has global scope and can be accessed anywhere in the program.
It has local scope and cannot be accessed outside the function.
It is accessible globally if defined with the def keyword.
It has the same scope as variables defined outside any function.
artifact.ex: The correct choice is that a variable created inside a function has local scope and cannot be accessed outside the function. The misconception is believing that variables defined inside a function retain global scope, which is incorrect.

claims: Every Python value has a data type (such as int, float, or str); expressions combine values, and conversion functions move a value from one type to another.
The interpreter performs implicit type conversion to promote types automatically inside a mixed expression.
int() converts a value to an integer and removes any fractional part, so int(3.9) is 3.
True division (/) converts numbers to floats before dividing and always returns a float.
Floor division (//) computes the whole-number quotient, discarding the remainder.

artifact.df: The automatic type promotion performed by the interpreter within a mixed expression.
artifact.eg: A mixed expression involving an int and a float will result in a float.
artifact.mi: Assuming the interpreter only performs explicit type changes when functions are called.
artifact.cx: Recognizing that the interpreter performs implicit type conversion to promote types automatically inside a mixed expression.

artifact.df: An integer-style quotient that drops any remainder.
artifact.eg: In `7 // 2`, the result is `3`, which is the whole-number quotient.
artifact.mi: It means dividing and then rounding to the nearest whole number.
artifact.cx: The operation discards the remainder rather than rounding; the related decimal-producing operator is `/`.

artifact.q: Which structure executes code only when a specific test evaluates to true?
artifact.ex: The if statement runs its body only when the condition is true. Misconception: Thinking the if statement runs the body regardless of the condition. Correction: The if statement skips the body when the condition is false.

artifact.q: In a short Python program, you want to print a reminder only when the user enters a value greater than 10. Which control-flow structure fits best?
artifact.ex: A plain if statement fits because it runs its body only when the condition is true. The common misconception is to pick a loop or exception handler for every decision, but those structures solve different problems.

artifact.q: If a string $s$ has a length of 5, what is the index of the right-most character?
artifact.ex: Option 4 is incorrect because the right-most character is at index len(s) - 1, which is 4 for a string of length 5. Option 2 is correct because the right-most character is at index len(s) - 1, which is 4 for a string of length 5.

artifact.q: In Python, if s = "studio", which expression returns the substring "tud"?
artifact.ex: s[1:4] is correct because slicing includes the start index 1 and stops before index 4, giving characters at positions 1, 2, and 3. The most plausible mistake is choosing s[0:3], which also has three characters but starts one position too early and returns "stu" instead.

artifact.ex: [12, 15, 18] is correct because a list is written with square brackets holding comma-separated values. The parenthesized choice is a tuple-shaped misconception, while braces suggest a different container.

artifact.df: Names that are treated as different when their letters use different capitalization.

artifact.mi: Changing only capitalization leaves the name unchanged.
artifact.cx: Python distinguishes total from Total, so the capitalization matters.

artifact.ex: A conditional statement chooses which block of code to run based on whether a condition is true. Misconception: Assuming the conditional statement always executes the true block. Correction: The conditional statement chooses which block of code to run based on whether a condition is true.

artifact.q: A program should show one message when a test score is passing and a different message when it is not. Which structure matches that behavior?
artifact.ex: An if-else statement matches because it chooses exactly one branch: the if body when the condition is true, or the else body when it is false. A likely misconception is that a single if can cover both outcomes, but it skips its body when the condition is false.

claims: Recursion solves a problem by reducing it to a simpler version of the same problem; a recursive function calls itself on a smaller input until it reaches a base case.
A recursive function calls itself on a smaller input.
The process continues until the problem is small enough that the solution is known or easily found — the base case.
Without a base case that stops the self-calls, recursion never terminates and overflows the call stack.
attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §12.1 Recursion basics

artifact.df: A way to solve a problem by turning it into a smaller version of the same problem until a base case is reached.
artifact.eg: A function that counts down from 5 by calling itself with 4, then 3, then 2, until it reaches 0.
artifact.mi: Recursion just means using many loops to do the same task.
artifact.cx: A recursive solution can use self-calls on smaller inputs, while loops repeat without self-calls.

artifact.df: The specific state or input size that signals the end of the recursive process.
artifact.eg: In calculating the factorial of 0, the function immediately returns 1 because 0 is the base case.
artifact.mi: Thinking the termination condition is the final result of the calculation.
artifact.cx: The termination condition is the base case, which is the point where the solution is known or easily found.

claims: Recursion solves a problem by reducing it to a simpler version of the same problem; a recursive function calls itself on a smaller input until it reaches a base case.
A recursive function calls itself on a smaller input.

artifact.q: A student writes a function to sum numbers from n down to 1 by calling the same function on n-1. What feature must be present so the program eventually stops?
op: A stopping condition for a small enough input
A loop counter that increases forever
A second function that replaces every call
A print statement after each call
artifact.ex: A stopping condition is the base case: it ends the self-calls once the input is small enough. The common misconception is that recursion stops just because the input changes; without a base case, the calls continue instead of terminating.

artifact.q: What is the fundamental mechanism by which a recursive function progresses toward a solution?
op: A) Iteratively applying a transformation until a condition is met.
b) Calling itself with a larger input until a stop condition is reached.
C) Reducing the problem to a simpler version until a known solution is found.
D) Storing the result in a loop variable for later use.
artifact.ex: Option C is correct because recursion solves a problem by reducing it to a simpler version of the same problem until a base case is reached. Option B is a misconception because recursive functions call themselves on a *smaller* input, not a larger one.

claims: A dictionary stores key-value pairs and looks up each value by its key rather than by a numeric position.

artifact.df: The constraint that every identifier used to access a stored item must be distinct.

artifact.df: A label used to retrieve one stored value from a mapping.
artifact.eg: In a dictionary of course rooms, 'BIO101' can point to one room assignment.
artifact.mi: A key can repeat many times for the same mapping entry.
artifact.cx: Because lookup uses labels, the same key cannot be duplicated in one dictionary.

claims: A dictionary stores key-value pairs and looks up each value by its key rather than by a numeric position.

artifact.q: A lab group needs to store student test scores under each student’s name and retrieve a score later by name. Which structure best fits that task?
op: A table with only repeated labels
A single value with no labels
artifact.ex: A collection of key-value pairs is correct because the data is labeled and values are retrieved by key rather than by numeric position. The numbered-sequence choice fits ordered positions better, which is the common misconception here.

artifact.q: Which data structure is best suited for representing data where items are naturally labeled rather than ordered?
op: List, because it maintains a numeric position.
Dictionary, because it uses key-value pairs.
Tuple, because it enforces a fixed order.
Array, because it stores sequential data.
artifact.ex: The correct choice is Dictionary because it is ideal when data is naturally labeled rather than ordered. A common misconception is choosing a List because it maintains a numeric position, which is incorrect as lists are ordered by index.

Binds count to the value produced on the right
Creates two variables with the same name
Deletes the old value stored in count

C: It binds the name on the left to the value produced on the right.
D: It creates a new, independent copy of the value on the right.
artifact.ex: Option C is correct because the assignment operator binds the name on the left to the value produced on the right. Option B is a misconception because assignment is not mathematical equality; it copies a value rather than asserting two sides are equal.

Retrieving objects of a container one at a time.
Iterating over each element of a container.

It stores the whole word inside the loop variable at once.
It changes the word into a range of integers automatically.
